The figures in @tbl-firms-data are assembled as follows. For the Anthropic-like frontier lab, revenue is \$386M in 2024 and \$4.59B in 2025, and CapEx is 2025 compute spending of \$7.33B, all as reported by the press from the company's draft IPO prospectus (September 2026); these replace earlier run-rate-based press estimates (\$0.9B for 2024). Annualized run rates have since grown far faster than recognized revenue: the company reported more than \$47B in May 2026, and the press reported \$65B by the end of July and quarterly revenue of about \$11.5B in Q2 2026. For the OpenAI-like platform, revenue is \$3.7B in 2024 and \$13.1B in 2025, the latter from press reports of the company's audited financial statements; the CFO's January 2026 post gives annualized run rates of \$2B, \$6B, and \$20B+ for 2023--2025 and does not itself report recognized revenue, so the two series are not interchangeable (the run-rate series would raise the 2025 figure and lower the CapEx/Revenue ratio below one). CapEx is \$12B of Azure inference and training spend, an operating commitment to cloud capacity rather than owned infrastructure. For the Google-like hyperscaler, revenue is Google Cloud revenue (\$43.2B in 2024, growing 37--39\% to \$59--60B in 2025 per the Alphabet SEC filing) rather than Alphabet-wide revenue (\$403B), and CapEx is total Alphabet capital expenditure (\$91.4B in 2025), approximately 60\% to servers and 40\% to data centers and networking. For the xAI-like compute racer,^[This illustration describes xAI's standalone AI business before its acquisition by SpaceX, announced in February 2026 at a combined valuation of \$1.25 trillion (\url{https://www.reuters.com/business/musks-spacex-merge-with-xai-combined-valuation-125-trillion-bloomberg-news-2026-02-02/}). SpaceX listed in June 2026, and in 2026 its AI segment began selling large blocks of compute to other laboratories, with one customer accounting for 59.5\% of segment revenue in Q2 2026 (SpaceX Form 10-Q). The combined firm is therefore no longer a pure compute racer, and the archetype should be read as a pre-merger snapshot.] revenue is 2025 standalone AI revenue (AI solutions, subscriptions, and data licensing, about \$0.92B) and CapEx is 2025 AI capital expenditure (\$12.7B), both from SpaceX's Form S-1 (May 2026). The AI segment reported in that filing also includes X advertising (segment revenue \$3.2B), which falls outside the model's scope. The Google-like archetype's CapEx/Revenue ratio of 1.52$\times$ uses consolidated CapEx as the numerator because Alphabet's infrastructure spending supports AI workloads across all products rather than the Cloud segment alone; a segment-level ratio using only Cloud-attributed CapEx would be lower (approximately 0.5--0.7$\times$) but would understate the total AI infrastructure investment that the model's capacity $K$ represents. Revenue and CapEx are therefore not defined identically across the four archetypes, which is why @sec-calibration reads the columns of @tbl-firms and @tbl-firms-data one at a time rather than as cross-sectional moments.

**Evidence behind the training fractions $\hat{\phi}$.** The values of $\hat{\phi}$ in @tbl-firms are assigned judgmentally, guided by three types of evidence; no moment is matched.

*Executive statements.* @amodei2026dwarkesh modeled the long-run equilibrium at "roughly 50/50 training and inference," noting that "it's not gonna be 10\%, it's not gonna be 90\%." Two further statements point the same way, both reported in the trade press rather than in company filings: Microsoft's CFO described Azure AI revenue as "primarily inference and post-training workloads," and Jensen Huang estimated that inference workloads would require "easily 100 times more" compute than anticipated, with inference accounting for more than 40\% of AI-related revenue by late 2025.

*Firm-specific data.* The only company-level decomposition I could locate is Epoch AI's reconstruction of OpenAI's 2024 compute, a secondary source assembled from investor documents shared with journalists in September 2024 and from press reports: of approximately \$7B in total cloud compute, roughly \$3B went to training, \$1.8B to inference, and about \$1B per year to research and experimentation, which Epoch AI amortizes over an assumed two years to arrive at roughly \$2B.^[\url{https://epoch.ai/data-insights/openai-compute-spend}. Epoch AI cautions that the underlying figures rely on projections for the final quarter of 2024 and should not be treated as fully reliable.] On that reconstruction, combined R\&D (training plus research) was approximately 71\% and inference approximately 26\%. Epoch AI's own reading is that most of the R\&D compute likely went to research, experimental training runs, and training runs for unreleased models rather than to the final training runs of released models; the model's $\hat{\phi}$ subsumes both.

No 2026 disclosure that I could locate breaks out training and inference compute for any of the four firms. Epoch AI's May 2026 estimates of frontier-lab compute stocks (about 1.7 million H100-equivalents for OpenAI and 1 million for Anthropic at the end of 2025) do not split them either.^[\url{https://epoch.ai/gradient-updates/frontier-labs-dont-use-most-ai-compute}.] The $\hat{\phi}$ values are therefore unchanged from the earlier evidence.

*Industry trajectory.* Deloitte's TMT Predictions 2026 estimates that the industry-wide split shifted from roughly two-thirds training to parity (approximately 50/50) in 2025, and is projected to reach two-thirds inference by 2026, driven by expanding user bases, reasoning models using 10--100 times more compute per query, and enterprise adoption at scale.^[\url{https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/technology/technology-media-and-telecom-predictions.html}.]

**Archetype-specific rationale.** The xAI-like compute racer allocates the most to training ($\hat{\phi} = 0.75$), consistent with xAI's 2025 strategy of dedicating owned compute (the Colossus supercluster) to frontier model training while outsourcing inference to cloud providers; since the SpaceX merger, part of that capacity has been leased to other laboratories, which the pre-merger archetype does not reflect. The Google-like hyperscaler allocates the least ($\hat{\phi} = 0.35$), meant to capture the need to serve inference to billions of users across Search, Gmail, and YouTube; Google's seventh-generation Ironwood TPU is designed for inference workloads. The Anthropic-like and OpenAI-like archetypes fall between these extremes.

**The belief inversion.** The moderate elasticity of $\phi^*$ with respect to $\lambda$ ($\varepsilon \approx +0.5$ at baseline, reflecting $\varepsilon_{\phi^*,\lambda} = (1-\phi^*)/(1-\alpha)$) means the inverse mapping $\lambda(\hat{\phi})$ is steep: modest uncertainty in the assigned training fraction ($\pm 0.10$) translates into a wide range of implied arrival rates. Inverting the closed-form allocation first-order condition, $\lambda = (\hat{\phi}/(1-\hat{\phi}))^{1-\alpha}(r - \mu_H)$, for each archetype at $\hat{\phi} \pm 0.10$ yields implied arrival rates spanning roughly a factor of two: the xAI-like archetype implies $\lambda \in [0.09, 0.17]$ (expected horizons of 6--11 years), while the Google-like hyperscaler implies $\lambda \in [0.03, 0.05]$ (19--32 years). Two qualifications apply. First, this inversion holds the discount rate at the common baseline $r = 0.12$; because the implied $\lambda$ scales with $r - \mu_H$, using archetype-specific WACCs would shift the levels materially and widen rather than narrow the cross-sectional dispersion (the xAI-like archetype at $r = 0.18$ implies $\lambda \in [0.17, 0.34]$, the Google-like archetype at $r = 0.10$ implies $\lambda \in [0.02, 0.04]$). Second, the ordering claim applies to common perturbations of the $\hat{\phi}$ values: the baseline ordering, xAI-like $>$ OpenAI-like $>$ Anthropic-like $>$ Google-like in implied $\lambda$, is preserved when all $\hat{\phi}$ shift together, but the $\pm 0.10$ bands of adjacent archetypes overlap, so independent errors could reorder neighboring pairs (though not the endpoints). Because the $\hat{\phi}$ values are assigned rather than measured, the inversion is a scenario map from allocations to the beliefs that would rationalize them within the model, not evidence that beliefs explain observed differences across firms.

**Archetype outputs under the model of record.** @tbl-archetypes evaluates the model at each archetype's implied belief, at $\hat{\phi}$ and at $\hat{\phi} \pm 0.10$. Every parameter other than $\lambda$ is at the baseline, the discount rate included: three of the four archetype WACCs (0.14, 0.15 and 0.18) lie outside the window $r \in (0.097, 0.135)$ on which (A2) holds, so the capacity problem is not well-posed at them, and only the Google-like WACC of $0.10$ lies inside it. The inversion at the archetype's own WACC, which needs no capacity, gives the bands of the previous paragraph. The credit columns price debt issued at the precommitted-scale entry $(X^*, K^*, \phi^*)$ at the archetype's leverage, with the exact claims and recovery rule of Internet Appendix H, under the archetype's own belief. The loss columns value the archetype's policy under the baseline $\lambda = 0.10$, as in Numerical Finding 1. The patterns are those summarized in @sec-calibration: waiting for the switch, with scale chosen at it, at every belief from $0.073$ up; a precommitted-scale trigger and capacity that are hump-shaped in $\lambda$ and fall sharply only in the Google-like band; and default probabilities and losses that rise toward the pessimistic end. Two features of the low beliefs bear on the reading. The precommitted-scale triggers at the lower end of the Google-like band and at its $\hat{\phi}$, $0.00054$ and $0.0034$, lie below the reference demand $X_0 = 0.0046$ at which the losses are measured, so from $X_0$ those firms invest at once, at the scale their belief prescribes there (the convention of Numerical Finding 1). And at those two beliefs the trigger with scale chosen at the switch is close to the precommitted-scale one ($0.00054$ and $0.0036$), while from $\lambda \approx 0.05$ up it lies several times above it and diverges as $\lambda$ approaches $0.073$ ($1.2$ at the Anthropic-like $\hat{\phi}$). The duopoly is not re-solved at the archetype beliefs. The cached equilibria of the entry game at zero leverage (@tbl-duopoly-beliefs) include five arrival rates that fall inside a band: $0.05$ in the Google-like band, where first investment is $X_L = 0.00084$ with $K_L = 0.00049$ and $\phi_L = 0.37$; $0.075$ in the Anthropic-like and OpenAI-like bands ($X_L = 0.0023$, $K_L = 0.0022$, $\phi_L = 0.56$); and $0.10$ and $0.15$ in the xAI-like band ($X_L = 0.0034$ and $0.0038$, $K_L = 0.0042$ and $0.0056$, $\phi_L = 0.68$ and $0.81$).

**Stated and implied beliefs.** A statement that the switch arrives with probability $p$ within $T$ years maps into a constant arrival rate through $P(\tau \leq T) = 1 - e^{-\lambda T}$, so $\lambda = -\ln(1-p)/T$ and the expected waiting time is $1/\lambda$. @tbl-stated-beliefs applies the mapping to the probabilities stated in @amodei2026dwarkesh and evaluates the allocation rule there. The "hunch" is an even chance that the capabilities arrive in "one to two, maybe more like one to three" years, which I read as $p = 0.5$ at the upper end of each range; reading it at one year would give $\lambda = 0.69$. The same interview gives the "roughly 50/50" split of compute between training and inference quoted above, which inverts to $\lambda = 0.06$ at $r = 0.12$, against the $0.23$ to $0.46$ of the timelines. @sec-calibration discusses the readings of this gap.

**Training-inference boundary.** The boundary between "training" and "inference" is also blurring. Inference-time scaling (chain-of-thought reasoning, search-augmented generation, and agentic workflows) uses inference hardware to produce capability improvements previously achievable only through training. The model treats $\hat{\phi}$ as a fixed allocation at investment time; in practice, firms dynamically reallocate GPUs between training and inference on timescales of weeks. What a lab cannot re-purpose at the switch is the capability already trained, not the compute, and the pre-positioned-capability extension of Internet Appendix E (@tbl-capability) solves the single firm's problem under that reading; @sec-discussion discusses the direction of the bias from holding the allocation fixed.

**Baseline policy.** Under the baseline calibration, the exact single-firm problem of Proposition 1 gives the training fraction $\phi^* \approx 0.70$ and, with the post-switch scale precommitted, the trigger $X^* \approx 0.0093$ and capacity $K^* \approx 0.0158$; with scale chosen at the switch the single firm waits for it (@tbl-baseline-results). The pure-power approximation gives $X^{\text{pp}} \approx 0.0047$ and $K^{\text{pp}} \approx 0.0067$ with the same $\phi^*$. In the entry game at zero leverage one firm invests first at $X_L \approx 0.0034$, with $K_L \approx 0.0042$ and $\phi_L \approx 0.68$, $64\%$ below the precommitted-scale single firm's trigger, and the other waits for the switch and enters at $X_F^* \approx 0.044$ with $K_F \approx 0.16$, all of it in training; the rent-equalization trigger $X_P \approx 0.0086$ is an upper bound on the date of first investment (@tbl-duopoly-beliefs). Proposition 3(i) characterizes the follower's post-switch scale, which is what makes the follower $39$ times larger than the leader.

**Normalization.** Because $c = 1$ fixes the cost scale by normalization (the same rescaling argument that makes the chosen $\delta$ part of the normalization rather than a separately identified quantity), the levels of $K$ and $X$ are not interpretable as physical units, and the quantitative content resides in ratios and percentages. Two operations that both bear on units should be kept apart. The first is a change of the cost scale, which re-solves the model. With $\kappa = c^{1/(\gamma-1)}$, substitute $K = \tilde{K}/\kappa$ and $X = \tilde{X}/\kappa^{1-\alpha}$: revenue $X K^\alpha$ becomes $\tilde{X}\tilde{K}^\alpha/\kappa$, the investment cost $cK^\gamma$ becomes $c^{1-\gamma/(\gamma-1)}\tilde{K}^\gamma = \tilde{K}^\gamma/\kappa$, and the operating cost $\delta K/r$ becomes $\delta\tilde{K}/(r\kappa)$, so the problem at cost $c$ is the problem at $c = 1$ with every payoff divided by $\kappa$. The optimal policy therefore transforms as $K \to K/\kappa$ and $X \to X/\kappa^{1-\alpha}$, and values scale by $1/\kappa$. The argument uses only the primitives, so it holds in the exact problem and in the entry game, whose contest shares depend on ratios of capacities. Every ratio and percentage reported in the paper is unchanged, and so are the credit objects of @sec-valuation and Internet Appendix H, because they are evaluated at the model's own policies, which transform with the units; re-solving the single firm at $c = 4$ reproduces the transformation, the distance to the boundary, the spread and the default probability to six digits. The second operation is a monetary unit $m$, the dollar value of one unit of value in the normalized model. It re-solves nothing and converts values only. Setting $m$ so that the leader's outlay at first investment, $I(K_L) = K_L^{1.5} \approx 0.00027$, equals the Anthropic-like archetype's 2025 compute spending of \$7.3B gives $m \approx \$27$ trillion; at that unit the follower's post-switch outlay, $I(K_F) \approx 0.066$, is about \$1.8 trillion, and matching the precommitted-scale single firm's outlay, $I(K^*) \approx 0.0020$, instead would give $m \approx \$3.7$ trillion.

**Comparative statics.** The statements here are for the precommitted-scale policy of the model of record (@tbl-elasticities). Higher volatility $\sigma$ increases the option value of waiting and raises the investment trigger, the standard real-options result that uncertainty raises the value of flexibility. A higher discount rate $r$ reduces the present value of future cash flows through $A_{\text{eff}}$ but also raises the characteristic root $\beta_H$, lowering the option premium ratio $\beta_H/(\beta_H - 1)$; at baseline the second effect dominates, so a higher $r$ lowers both the trigger and optimal capacity. Higher $\lambda$ increases the weight on H-regime revenue in $A_{\text{eff}}$ and shifts $\phi^*$ upward, so more optimistic firms allocate more compute to frontier model development; its effect on timing is not monotone, since the trigger rises with $\lambda$ up to about $0.13$ and falls beyond (@tbl-beliefs). Lower revenue elasticity $\alpha$ (stronger diminishing returns) reduces optimal capacity sharply and, because the smaller installation is cheaper to build and operate, lowers the trigger as well: at $\alpha = 0.38$ the trigger falls to $X^* \approx 0.0028$, and at $\alpha = 0.45$ it rises to $X^* \approx 0.083$, against the baseline $0.0093$. Internet Appendix E reports how the duopoly objects move across the joint sweep. @tbl-elasticities and Internet Appendices D and E report these magnitudes at the baseline and their robustness to joint perturbation; the signs, not the levels, are the model's disciplined prediction.

### D. Parameter Sensitivity {.unnumbered}

@tbl-elasticities reports the elasticities of the single firm's policy in the model of record with respect to each model parameter: the trigger $X^*$ and capacity $K^*$ of the precommitted-scale problem of Proposition 1(iii) and the training fraction $\phi^*$. They are computed numerically at the baseline calibration (function `policy_elasticities` of module `robustness.py`).

| Parameter | Symbol | Baseline | $\varepsilon_{X^*}$ | $\varepsilon_{K^*}$ | $\varepsilon_{\phi^*}$ |
|:----------|:------:|:--------:|:-------------------:|:-------------------:|:----------------------:|
| Discount rate | $r$ | 0.12 | $-21.6$ | $-28.2$ | $-1.0$ |
| Revenue elasticity | $\alpha$ | 0.40 | $+20.4$ | $+24.0$ | $+0.2$ |
| H-regime drift | $\mu_H$ | 0.06 | $+15.3$ | $+19.7$ | $+0.5$ |
| Volatility | $\sigma$ | 0.25 | $+9.6$ | $+11.8$ | $0$ |
| Cost convexity | $\gamma$ | 1.50 | $+3.1$ | $+6.6$ | $0$ |
| Operating cost rate | $\delta$ | 0.03 | $+2.2$ | $+2.0$ | $0$ |
| Arrival rate | $\lambda$ | 0.10 | $+0.2$ | $+0.5$ | $+0.5$ |

: Elasticities of the single firm's trigger, capacity, and training fraction with respect to model parameters. $X^*$ and $K^*$ are the trigger and capacity of the precommitted-scale problem of the model of record (Proposition 1(iii)) and $\phi^*$ the closed-form training fraction. For a parameter $\theta$, $\varepsilon_{X^*} = \partial \ln X^* / \partial \ln \theta$, and $\varepsilon_{K^*}$ and $\varepsilon_{\phi^*}$ are defined analogously; all are central differences in logs at the baseline values with a relative step of $0.1\%$, the policy being re-solved at each step. A "$0$" marks a parameter that does not enter the first-order condition for $\phi^*$. {#tbl-elasticities tbl-colwidths="[22,10,12,14,14,14]"}

The discount rate $r$ and revenue elasticity $\alpha$ are the most influential parameters for trigger and capacity, consistent with their central roles in real-options theory (the cost of waiting) and the production technology (the value of capacity). These are local elasticities at a baseline that sits close to the upper bound of the interior-capacity condition (A2), where capacity is steep in the parameters (Internet Appendix E states the window); elasticities of $20$ to $28$ mean that a $1\%$ change in $r$ or $\alpha$ moves capacity by a quarter, so the trigger and capacity levels are not a robust quantitative prediction of the model. The elasticities of the post-switch policy $(X_H^*, K_H^*)$, which is also the capacity of the pure-power approximation, are close to these ($-20.7$ and $-28.8$ for $r$, $+19.5$ and $+24.2$ for $\alpha$), with one difference: $K_H^*$ and $X_H^*$ do not respond to $\lambda$ at all, while the pre-switch capacity does ($+0.5$). The training fraction $\phi^*$ is insensitive to most parameters. Its first-order condition involves the parameters only through the ratio $w_H/w_L = \lambda/(r - \mu_H)$ and the revenue elasticity $\alpha$, so $\phi^*$ responds to $\lambda$ ($\varepsilon = +0.5$), $\mu_H$ ($\varepsilon = +0.5$), $r$ ($\varepsilon = -1.0$), and, weakly, $\alpha$ ($\varepsilon = +0.2$). Volatility $\sigma$, cost convexity $\gamma$, and the operating cost rate $\delta$ do not enter the training-allocation first-order condition at all.

### E. Robustness {.unnumbered}

Six exercises assess robustness. The first states where the capacity problem is well-posed and perturbs the calibrated parameters, one at a time and jointly, re-computing the objects the paper's qualitative claims rest on in the model of record. The second asks how much the duopoly results depend on the Tullock contest form, and quantifies the part of that question an arithmetic-mean industry-revenue benchmark can answer. The third quantifies the bias from holding the training fraction static, and the fourth solves an extension in which capability, not compute, has to be in place at the switch. The fifth computes the belief mismatch inside the entry equilibrium. The sixth asks what a three-regime capability ladder would change; that exercise is qualitative, as is the Cournot discussion inside the second.

**Where the capacity problem is well-posed.** The scale choice sets a pure-power revenue, proportional to $K^\alpha$, against a cost $\delta K/r + cK^\gamma$ that is linear at small scale and a power at large scale. After the switch the firm maximizes $a(K)^{\beta_H}/b(K)^{\beta_H - 1}$ with $a \propto K^\alpha$ and $b$ that cost, so an interior capacity exists if and only if the option-adjusted revenue elasticity $\alpha\beta_H/(\beta_H-1)$ lies strictly between the elasticities of the cost at its two ends, $1$ and $\gamma$, which is condition (A2), $1/\gamma < (\beta_H-1)/(\alpha\beta_H) < 1$. When the upper bound of (A2) fails the linear term is too weak to stop the firm shrinking toward zero scale, and when the lower bound fails the convex term is too weak to stop it growing without limit. The model of record does not widen this window. Every pre-switch object in it, the precommitted-scale policy, the value of waiting and the entry game, is built on the post-switch scale problem, which is unchanged, so the admissible region is the one (A2) implies. At the baseline values of the other parameters it is $r \in (0.097, 0.135)$, $\mu_H \in (0.051, 0.077)$, $\sigma \in (0.190, 0.392)$, $\alpha \in (0.356, 0.534)$ and $\gamma > 1.124$; the parameters $\mu_L$, $\lambda$, $\delta$ and $c$ do not enter (A2). The entry game needs $\alpha < 1/2$ in addition, for a unique capacity on the exercise envelope. Inside the window the problem is well-posed but steep: capacity goes to zero at one edge and to infinity at the other, which is where the elasticities of $20$ to $28$ in @tbl-elasticities come from. The two sweeps below measure what this does to the paper's objects (module `robustness.py`; `just run-sweep`).

**One-at-a-time sweep.** I perturb each of the nine calibrated parameters ($r$, $\mu_L$, $\mu_H$, $\sigma$, $\lambda$, $\alpha$, $\gamma$, $\delta$, and $c$) one at a time by $\pm 25\%$ from the baseline, giving eighteen draws, and re-solve at each draw the single firm of the model of record: the allocation $\phi^*$ and the thresholds $\underline{\phi}$ and $\tilde{\phi}$, the precommitted-scale policy $(X^*, K^*)$, whether the firm that chooses its scale at the switch invests before it, and Dario's dilemma in the three metrics of @tbl-dilemma-pairs with the draw's own arrival rate as the truth. Draws that leave the admissible region are reported with the condition they violate and are not dropped.

Five of the eighteen draws violate (A2). Four fail through its upper bound: $r = 0.15$, $\mu_H = 0.045$, $\sigma = 0.188$, and $\alpha = 0.30$. The fifth, $r = 0.09$, violates the lower bound, so both directions of the $\pm 25\%$ range for $r$ fall outside the window. A sixth draw, $\gamma = 1.125$, clears the lower bound by $0.001$ and is inside the window, but the optimal capacity there lies above the range the solver searches ($K$ up to $e^{15}$), and I report it as unsolved. Twelve draws are solved.

Across those twelve, $\phi^* \in [0.59, 0.79]$, $\underline{\phi} \in [0.10, 0.23]$ and $\tilde{\phi} \in [0.19, 0.37]$, and the ordering $0 < \underline{\phi} < \tilde{\phi} < \phi^*$ holds in every draw. The firm that chooses its scale at the switch waits for it in eleven draws; at $\gamma = 1.875$ the ratio of the value of waiting to the exercise envelope at high demand falls to $0.997$ (baseline $1.08$) and the firm has a finite pre-switch trigger, at a demand about a thousand times the precommitted-scale trigger. For the precommitted-scale version of the dilemma, the pessimistic loss exceeds the optimistic loss in every draw for equal errors in $\lambda$ (ratio between $18.7$ and $27.5$, baseline $24.6$) and for equal errors in $\log\lambda$ (between $1.8$ and $2.8$ at a factor of five, baseline $2.4$; between $1.7$ and $7.2$ at a factor of $1.8$, baseline $3.3$). For equal errors in expected years the baseline ranking, in which the optimist loses slightly more (ratio $0.78$), holds in eleven draws and reverses at $\lambda = 0.075$ (ratio $1.58$). With scale chosen at the switch the pessimist loses between $36\%$ and $53\%$ and the optimist at $1.8\lambda$ loses nothing. The parameters $\delta$ and $c$ only set the cost scale, in which the value functions are homogeneous (@sec-calibration), so they move $X^*$ and $K^*$ and leave every ratio and share at its baseline value. The scale-gap index of Internet Appendix G, which is defined at the pure-power policy, stays between $50\%$ and $59\%$ at one tenth of that capacity and between $25\%$ and $30\%$ at three tenths.

The entry game of @sec-duopoly is re-solved at zero leverage at each draw that is admissible for it, and compared with the single firm at the same draw. Of the twelve solved draws, $\alpha = 0.50$ lies outside the game's domain, and at $\mu_H = 0.075$ the game has no rent-equalization trigger on the demand scan: following is worth more than leading at every scanned demand level, by at least $4\%$, and leading is worth at most $0.98$ of mutual waiting, so on the scan neither firm invests before the switch (also on the wider scan for $X_L$, where leading is worth at most $0.98$ of mutual waiting). In the ten other draws the equilibrium of Proposition 3(iii) passes its no-deviation checks and every qualitative statement about it holds: the first investment $X_L$ is between $0.27$ and $0.40$ of the precommitted-scale trigger $X^*$ (baseline $0.36$) and between $0.26$ and $0.58$ of $X_P$ ($0.39$); the leader installs between $0.17$ and $0.31$ of $K^*$ ($0.26$) and trains with between $0.93$ and $0.99$ of $\phi^*$ ($0.97$); the follower's post-switch trigger is between $5.7$ and $42$ times $X_L$ ($13$); and following is worth between $1.05$ and $1.17$ times leading at $X_L$ ($1.10$). The draws of $\delta$ and $c$ reproduce the baseline ratios to three digits.

*The cell $\gamma = 1.9$.* The diagnostic that preceded the choice of the model of record found the game close to a knife edge at $\gamma = 1.9$ when the leader's scale was held fixed, and I report that cell here (it lies just outside the $\pm 25\%$ range, which ends at $1.875$). With the leader choosing its scale the equilibrium exists and passes its checks at both values: at $\gamma = 1.9$, $X_L$ is $0.33$ of $X^*$ and $0.24$ of $X_P$, the leader installs $0.24$ of $K^*$, and following is worth $1.17$ times leading. Three properties of the baseline do not carry over. The single firm with scale chosen at the switch no longer waits (the waiting margin is $0.993$), although its trigger is about $300$ times $X^*$. The difference $L^* - F$ changes sign twice on the scan, at $\gamma = 1.875$ as well, so $X_P$ is the first of two crossings and not the only one. And at $\gamma = 1.9$ the follower no longer waits for the switch at every demand level: it would enter before the switch at a demand several hundred thousand times $X_L$, which is of no practical consequence but is a different best response.

**Joint sweep.** One-at-a-time perturbations do not search the joint parameter space, so I also draw all nine parameters together: $4{,}096$ points of a scrambled Sobol sequence with a fixed seed in the box of $\pm 25\%$ around the baseline. Of these, $2{,}179$ ($53.2\%$) lie outside the window, $1{,}286$ through the upper bound of (A2) and $893$ through the lower bound. Of the $1{,}917$ inside it, seven are not solved because an optimum lies above the capacity range searched (six in the precommitted-scale problem, one in the problem with scale chosen at the switch), and $1{,}910$ are solved. @tbl-joint-sweep reports the distribution of each object over the solved draws. It is a statement about that box and those draws, not about the parameter space at large.

The objects in @tbl-joint-sweep separate into three groups. The allocation and the thresholds are stable: $\phi^*$ stays between $0.53$ and $0.85$ in nine draws out of ten, and the ordering $0 < \underline{\phi} < \tilde{\phi} < \phi^*$ holds in $1{,}894$ of the $1{,}910$ draws ($99.2\%$); the sixteen exceptions, in which $\tilde{\phi}$ exceeds $\phi^*$, have $\lambda \leq 0.093$ together with $r \geq 0.134$ and $\mu_H \leq 0.053$, a low ratio $\lambda/(r - \mu_H)$. Levels are not stable: the capacity $K^*$ covers almost thirteen orders of magnitude across the solved draws and six between the $5\%$ and $95\%$ quantiles, the counterpart in the joint sweep of the elasticities of @tbl-elasticities. The error of the pure-power approximation is large in every draw, between $20\%$ and $66\%$ in the trigger and between $27\%$ and $75\%$ in capacity, always downward.

The qualitative statements about the single firm survive unevenly. That the firm with scale chosen at the switch waits for it holds in $1{,}645$ draws ($86.1\%$); in the other $265$ it has a finite pre-switch trigger, and these are concentrated at high cost convexity and long timelines ($242$ have $\gamma \geq 1.5$ and $218$ have $\lambda < 0.10$). For Dario's dilemma with precommitted scale, the pessimistic error is the costlier one in every solved draw for equal errors in $\lambda$ (the ratio is never below $9$) and for equal errors in $\log\lambda$ at a factor of five (never below $1.13$). At a factor of $1.8$ in logs it is the costlier one in $1{,}829$ draws ($95.8\%$) and the ranking reverses in $81$, of which $80$ have $\lambda \geq 0.10$. For equal errors in expected years the baseline ranking, in which the optimist loses more, holds in $1{,}373$ draws ($71.9\%$) and reverses in $537$, of which $499$ have $\lambda < 0.10$: the sign of the horizon comparison follows the arrival rate and is not a robust property. With scale chosen at the switch the pessimist at $0.2\lambda$ loses between $22\%$ and $63\%$, and the optimist at $1.8\lambda$ loses nothing in $1{,}647$ draws and at most $0.5\%$ in the others. These counts are the reproducible content of the robustness statements made elsewhere in this Internet Appendix about the single firm.

The entry game is solved on a subsample, because one equilibrium takes between three minutes and an hour: the first $64$ joint draws, in the order of the sequence, that satisfy (A2) and $\alpha < 1/2$. The first investment $X_L$ is located on a demand scan anchored at the single firm's triggers and not at $X_P$ (Proof of Proposition 3), so it is found also where the game has no rent-equalization trigger. In $59$ of the $64$ draws a firm invests before the switch on the scan, and @tbl-duopoly-sweep reports these $59$.

The quantiles of $X_L/X_P$ are over the $47$ draws with a rent-equalization trigger on the scan; its count includes the twelve draws without one, at which following is worth more than leading at every scanned demand level. The duopoly statements are less robust to joint perturbation than the single-firm ones, and less robust than the one-at-a-time sweep suggests. First, in $17$ of the $64$ draws ($27\%$) the game has no rent-equalization trigger on the demand scan: following is worth more than leading at every scanned demand level, by between $0.02\%$ and $21\%$ at the closest point. In twelve of them a firm whose rival follows invests before the switch, at a demand between $1.1$ and $995$ times $X_H^*$ (median $13$), and the equilibrium passes its checks in eight. In the other five, two of which lie next to the lower bound of (A2), leading is worth at most $0.98$ of mutual waiting everywhere on the scan, so no firm invests before the switch there, and since the game after the switch is a race in each of them, neither firm gains on the scan by investing first. Second, among the $59$ draws with a first investment, $X_L$ precedes the single firm's precommitted-scale trigger in $48$ and follows it in eleven, where the leader is also larger than the single firm; six of the eleven are draws without a rent-equalization trigger, with $X_L$ between $5.6$ and $290$ times $X^*$. Third, $X_L$ lies below $X_P$, with following the better role at $X_L$, in $44$ of the $47$ draws with a rent-equalization trigger; in the other three $X_L$ exceeds $X_P$ by between $1.5\%$ and $7\%$, the follower would rather lead, and the first investment is at $X_P$, the outcome of a race and not of a second-mover advantage. Fourth, in eight draws the game after the switch is not a race, so the value of mutual waiting that defines $X_L$ rests on a continuation that does not apply. Fifth, in one draw without a rent-equalization trigger on the coarser scan for $X_P$, leading beats following by $0.03\%$ at a point of the scan for $X_L$ above $X_L$, so the follower's off-path condition fails there. The no-deviation checks therefore all hold in $47$ of the $59$ draws ($80\%$). The follower's post-switch trigger lies above $X_L$ in every such draw, and the follower waits for the switch at every demand level in $49$ of them; in the other ten it also has a pre-switch trigger, at a demand between $300$ and $14{,}000$ times $X_L$. What is robust on this subsample is that the leader enters small and early relative to the follower; that a firm invests before the switch, that it does so before the single firm, that following is the better role, and that the selected equilibrium exists in the form of Proposition 3(iii) hold in most draws and not in all.

**Alternative contest functions.** The Tullock contest is a reduced form, so the concern is that the duopoly results are artifacts of its functional form. I do not solve the Cournot alternative, and the two paragraphs that follow are qualitative; what I quantify instead is the role of the Tullock form's revenue-expansion property. The main qualitative mechanisms do not depend on the contest functional form, because each operates through the composition of $A_{\text{eff}}$: the faith-based survival mechanism (Proposition 2) requires only that the default boundary take the form $X_D = [\beta_L^-/(\beta_L^- - 1)] \cdot (C_D/r + \delta K_i/r) / A_{\text{eff},i}$ with $\partial A_{\text{eff},i}/\partial \lambda > 0$ for $\phi_i > \underline{\phi}$, conditions that do not reference how revenue shares are determined; and the Dario's dilemma asymmetry operates through the single-firm training allocation channel, which involves no contest at all. The preemption incentive is likely weaker under a Cournot specification, in which firms choose quantities and price clears the market, because capacity differences translate less directly into revenue differences: under Tullock, a capacity advantage maps directly to a larger revenue share ($s_i \propto K_i^\alpha$), whereas under Cournot, additional capacity lowers the equilibrium price, partially offsetting the quantity gain.

The quantified check uses an *arithmetic-mean industry-revenue benchmark*: shares remain Tullock, but the revenue of a market is the arithmetic mean of the standalone revenues of the firms active in it, so a firm facing an active rival earns $s_i \cdot (y_i + y_j)/2 = y_i/2$, half its standalone revenue, where $y_i = [(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha$ in the inference market and $y_i = (\phi_i K_i)^\alpha$ in the training market; a firm alone in a market earns $y_i$. Under symmetry this coincides exactly with the Tullock payoff. Under asymmetry it removes two things at once: the quadratic-mean revenue expansion, and the dependence of a firm's post-entry revenue on its rival's capacity, since $y_i/2$ does not involve $y_j$ (the pie itself still moves with both capacities, so this is not a fixed prize). The comparison therefore bounds the contribution of pie expansion from above and does not isolate it; a benchmark with a genuinely exogenous prize, or a Cournot market, would be needed to separate the two. @tbl-fixedpie reports the comparison at two layers, which should not be mixed: the exact primitives of the model of record, where the benchmark can be evaluated but its entry equilibrium cannot be constructed, and the nested pure-power game of Internet Appendix B, where the earlier draft solved it.

: The Tullock contest and the arithmetic-mean industry-revenue benchmark at the baseline calibration and zero leverage. The benchmark keeps Tullock shares but sets the revenue of a market to the arithmetic mean of the standalone revenues of the firms active in it, so a firm facing an active rival earns half its standalone revenue. Exact primitives: the follower's post-switch trigger (in units of the single firm's post-switch trigger $X_H^*$) and capacity are its best response, on the claims with the option to stop, to the leader of the benchmark equilibrium of the model of record, $(K_L, \phi_L) = (0.0042, 0.68)$; "leading over following" is the value of entering first after the switch, at the capacity that is best for the leader at that demand, over the value of following it, on thirteen log-spaced demand levels between $0.01$ and $100$ times $X_H^*$; the post-switch game is a race when following is the better role at the bottom of that scan and leading is at least as good above some demand level. Nested pure-power game: the reduced-form game of Internet Appendix B solved under each contest; $\phi_F^*$ is the follower's training fraction, $X_P/X^{\text{pp}}$ the rent-equalization trigger over the single firm's pure-power trigger, and $\underline{\phi}$ the threshold of @eq-phi-underbar. {#tbl-fixedpie tbl-colwidths="[50,22,25]"}

In the exact primitives two properties of the benchmark equilibrium of @sec-duopoly turn out to rest on the dependence of a firm's revenue on its rival's capacity. The first is the scale asymmetry. Under the Tullock form the follower answers the leader's training capacity with a capacity $39$ times as large and waits for a demand level $15.9$ times $X_H^*$; under the benchmark its problem does not involve the leader at all, and it enters at $1.9$ times $X_H^*$ with a capacity $1.6$ times the leader's. The second is the equilibrium itself. The first investment $X_L$ of Proposition 3(iii) is defined against the value $W$ of mutual waiting, which prices each firm at the follower's value in a post-switch race. Under the benchmark there is no such race: a firm that enters first after the switch keeps half its standalone revenue whatever its rival installs, so leading at the best scale is worth at least as much as following at every demand level scanned (between $1.00$ and $2.24$ times, against $0.71$ to $1.82$ under Tullock, where the crossing defines the race). The solver of the model of record therefore finds no post-switch rent-equalization trigger under the benchmark, and $X_L$ and $X_P$ are not computed for it. I do not conclude that the benchmark has no equilibrium with investment before the switch, only that it is not the equilibrium of Proposition 3(iii); the second-mover advantage at $X_L$ and the large follower are properties of a contest in which capacity takes revenue from the rival. Because the benchmark removes pie expansion and the rival-capacity channel together, the comparison cannot say which of the two is responsible.

In the nested pure-power game the training fraction and the faith-based survival threshold are identical across specifications: both depend on the balance between L-regime inference value and H-regime training value within $A_{\text{eff}}$, not on the revenue-expansion property. The trigger ratio is higher under the benchmark ($0.61$ against $0.56$ under Tullock), so the pull toward early entry is weaker. These two numbers are objects of the earlier draft's reduced-form game and are reported for continuity; they are not objects of the model of record, in which the single firm has no pure-power trigger to compare with. The single-firm Dario's dilemma involves no contest and is unaffected. The duopoly dilemma of @tbl-duopoly-dilemma is computed inside the Tullock equilibrium and has no counterpart under the benchmark.

**Dynamic training reallocation.** Holding $\phi$ fixed for the life of the project is a central limitation of the model, and the concern is that it biases $\phi^*$. To quantify the direction and magnitude of the bias, I solve a two-period extension in which the firm commits to $\phi_1$ at investment time and may revise the allocation once, at the end of the first period, conditioning on what it has observed: to $\phi_H$ if the regime switch has occurred by then, to $\phi_{L2}$ if it has not. After the revision the allocation is fixed forever, so each branch continues with the corresponding perpetuity. Capacity is held at $K^* = 0.0158$, the capacity of the single firm's precommitted-scale policy in the model of record, which isolates the allocation margin, and reallocation incurs a quadratic adjustment cost $\kappa \cdot (\Delta\phi)^2$ charged in the branch in which it occurs. All values in the exercise, including $\kappa$, are measured per unit of demand $X_0$ at the fixed capacity $K^*$, in the same units as the revenue coefficients; the static revenue value is $1.87$ per unit of $X_0$, so on the grid $\kappa \in \{0.5, 2, 10\}$ a full reversal of the baseline allocation ($\Delta\phi \approx 0.4$ at $\kappa = 0.5$) costs about $4\%$ of that value at the cheapest setting and $\kappa = 10$ makes any revision larger than a few points prohibitive, which spans the range from nearly free to effectively static. Writing $\rho = r - \mu_L + \lambda$ for the hazard-adjusted net discount rate of the L-regime (written $\Delta$ in the proof of Proposition 2), the value per unit of $X_0$ decomposes into the survival-adjusted L-regime flow over the first period (weight $(1 - e^{-\rho \, dt})/\rho$), the H-regime flow earned between an in-period switch and the revision date at the *pre-switch* allocation, the H perpetuity at the readjusted allocation in the switched state, and the L perpetuity at the readjusted allocation in the no-switch state (weight $e^{-\rho \, dt}$). The decomposition is exact rather than approximate: at $\phi_1 = \phi_H = \phi_{L2}$ the four terms collapse to the perpetual $A_{\text{eff}}$ of @eq-a-eff, so the $\kappa = \infty$ row is the static model itself and the value gains are measured against it.

| $\kappa$ | $\phi_1$ | $\phi_H$ | $\phi_{L2}$ | Value gain |
|:---------:|:--------:|:--------:|:-----------:|:----------:|
| 0 (free) | 0.01 | 0.99 | 0.70 | 5.1\% |
| 0.5 | 0.57 | 0.99 | 0.66 | 2.1\% |
| 2.0 | 0.68 | 0.99 | 0.69 | 1.1\% |
| 10.0 | 0.70 | 0.77 | 0.70 | 0.3\% |
| $\infty$ (static) | 0.70 | 0.70 | 0.70 | 0\% |

: Two-period dynamic reallocation at baseline ($\lambda = 0.10$, $dt = 1$ year). $\kappa$ is the quadratic reallocation cost parameter, charged as $\kappa (\Delta\phi)^2$ in the branch in which the revision occurs, so $\kappa = 0$ is free reallocation and $\kappa = \infty$ is the static model. $\phi_1$ is the training fraction chosen at investment, $\phi_H$ the fraction after a switch to regime $H$, and $\phi_{L2}$ the fraction after a first period with no switch. $\phi^* = 0.70$ in the static model; $\phi_1$ and $\phi_H$ are constrained to $[0.01, 0.99]$, and the $\kappa = 0$ row attains both bounds (the unconstrained optimum at $\kappa = 0$ is $\phi_1 \approx 0.007$, and the objective is nearly flat there). Capacity is held at $K^* = 0.0158$, the precommitted-scale capacity of the model of record; it enters only through the size of the adjustment cost relative to revenue, so the $\kappa = 0$ and $\kappa = \infty$ rows do not depend on it. Value gains are relative to the static revenue coefficient $A_{\text{eff}}(\phi^*, K^*)$. {#tbl-dynamic-phi tbl-colwidths="[15,15,15,15,15]"}

Three findings emerge. First, the option to revise pushes the initial allocation *below* the static optimum, by more the cheaper reallocation is: $\phi_1$ falls from $\phi^* = 0.70$ to $0.57$ at $\kappa = 0.5$ and to the lower bound of the admissible range when revision is free. The mechanism is that H-regime revenue in the model scales with the training capacity in place at the time, $A_H X (\phi K)^\alpha$, so a firm that can re-purpose compute once the switch is observed earns the H prize at its *initial* allocation only over the interval between the switch and the revision date, a state price of $0.003$ out of a total weight of $0.090$ on the switch payoff at a one-year period, about $3\%$. Almost the entire training motive is therefore deferred to the post-switch allocation. The static model, which forbids revision, is the polar case in which the whole H prize must be bought in advance; its $\phi^*$ is accordingly an *upper* bound on the pre-switch training fraction. The optimal allocation does not drift over time: $\phi_{L2} = \phi^* = 0.70$ exactly when $\kappa = 0$. Second, the value of the option is modest and is used mainly after the switch: the gain over the static allocation is $5.1\%$ of the gross revenue value at fixed capacity under free reallocation, falling to $0.3\%$ when adjustment costs are high, and the post-switch allocation goes to the training corner ($\phi_H = 0.99$ for $\kappa$ up to $2$). Third, and by way of scope, the exercise solves the allocation and the gross revenue value only; it does not solve the default problem or the belief-mismatch comparison under a revisable allocation, so it establishes nothing about the faith-based survival threshold or the Dario's dilemma asymmetry in a dynamic model. The static threshold $\underline{\phi} \approx 0.18$ of @eq-phi-underbar is a function of the parameters alone and is unaffected by construction. Note also that a $5\%$ gain in gross revenue value coexists with a large change in the very observable used to infer beliefs: under free reallocation the pre-switch training fraction collapses to the bound, so a small value distortion does not imply a small distortion in $\phi_1$ or in the $\lambda$ it would reveal.

These numbers bound the bias from one side. The exercise ties the H prize to the *contemporaneous* training capacity, which makes re-purposing maximally effective: nothing about the pre-switch allocation is embodied in the post-switch payoff. To the extent that post-switch revenue instead reflects capability accumulated from *cumulative* pre-switch training, the revision option is worth less and the static allocation is closer to optimal; in the limit where the prize is locked in at investment, the memoryless arrival and the absence of learning leave the continuation problem stationary and $\phi^*$ is exactly optimal. The gap also shrinks as the commitment period lengthens ($\phi_1 = 0.10$ at $\kappa = 0$ and $dt = 5$ years, against $0.01$ at $dt = 1$). @tbl-dynamic-phi therefore says that $\phi^*$ is the allocation of a firm that cannot cheaply and immediately re-purpose compute at the moment of the switch, and that the bias in the pre-switch training fraction runs downward, with a magnitude governed by the cost and speed of re-purposing and by how much of the H prize is embodied in prior training. Re-purposing is neither instantaneous nor free: the configuration, networking, and software investments specific to large training clusters keep the adjustment cost strictly positive. The stationarity of the problem rules out an alternative reading of the bias: the switch time is exponential and the firm learns nothing from its non-arrival, so conditional on no switch the problem after one period is identical to the problem at the investment date, with the hazard $\lambda$ unchanged and so is the continuation value that $\phi$ trades off against current inference revenue.^[An extension with unknown $\lambda$ and Bayesian learning would break this stationarity: non-arrival would lower the posterior arrival rate and generate a genuine downward drift in $\phi$ over time. The exercise here excludes that channel deliberately, so that what it measures is the value of re-purposing compute at the switch rather than the value of learning about $\lambda$.] Within this two-period, fixed-capacity, exponential-arrival exercise, the bias is therefore the value of the re-purposing option, and it has one immediate consequence for the calibration: because the static model overstates the pre-switch training fraction, the implied $\lambda$ that rationalizes a given $\hat{\phi}$ is *higher* under the dynamic model than under the static model, since $\hat{\phi}$ then represents a deliberate choice made despite the option to re-purpose rather than an irreversible commitment.

What dynamic reallocation would do to the paper's two headline mechanisms is not computed by the two-period exercise, and what follows is a conjecture conditional on how reallocation enters. The faith-based survival channel (Proposition 2) would be weakened, because a struggling firm could shift from training to inference to raise L-regime cash flow, partially offsetting the lower default boundary that a high $\phi$ buys. The channel survives to the extent that expected post-switch revenue reflects *cumulative* training investment rather than the compute currently allocated, so that $\phi$ continues to enter $A_{\text{eff}}$; in the opposite limit, where compute is re-purposed at the switch, the continuation-value floor remains, created by the option to move into training upon a switch, but it no longer varies with the firm's pre-switch $\phi$. For Dario's dilemma (Numerical Finding 1) two correction channels act on the gap between the two errors, in opposite directions. A firm that has over-trained can recover part of its loss by moving compute back to inference, which lowers the optimistic loss and, taken alone, widens the gap between the pessimistic and the optimistic loss. A firm that has under-trained can catch up by moving compute into training once the switch is observed, which lowers the pessimistic loss and, taken alone, narrows the gap. Which channel dominates depends on the cost and speed of each correction, so the direction of the net effect on the asymmetry is open; the extension below computes it for one technology. A full dynamic treatment with continuous $\phi_t$ control is left for future work.

**Pre-positioned capability.** The two-period exercise shows that the static $\phi^*$ rests on compute that cannot be re-purposed at the switch, and Internet Appendix C notes that labs reallocate GPUs between training and inference within weeks. This extension asks what the single firm does under a technology that is consistent with both: what cannot be bought at the switch is capability, not compute. It is an extension and not the model of record; none of the paper's other numbers uses it. Training capacity in place when the switch arrives counts in full in the post-switch market, and capability built afterwards counts at the rate $\kappa \in [0, 1]$, the *late-training effectiveness*, for incumbents and entrants alike (the symbol is reused: here and in @tbl-capability $\kappa$ is this effectiveness, not the adjustment cost of @tbl-dynamic-phi). An installed firm redeploys its inference capacity to training at the switch, so its post-switch revenue is $X[\phi K + \kappa(1-\phi)K]^\alpha$, and a firm that installs $K$ after the switch earns $X(\kappa K)^\alpha$. The case $\kappa = 0$ is a strict stock, in which a late entrant earns nothing, and $\kappa = 1$ is the flow economy with free redeployment, the case behind the first row of @tbl-dynamic-phi. The model of record is not a member of this family: its entrant has $\kappa = 1$ and its incumbent cannot redeploy. Everything else is as in the single-firm problem with scale chosen whenever the firm invests: the firm picks the trigger, the capacity and the allocation, and a firm without capacity at the switch keeps the option to enter. The stopping problem is solved exactly, as one scalar root for $(X^*, K^*)$ with the allocation in closed form (module `capability_stock.py`, function `capability_extension` of `robustness.py`).

The allocation maximizes $(1-\phi)^\alpha + \lambda A_H [\kappa + (1-\kappa)\phi]^\alpha$ with $A_H = 1/(r - \mu_H)$, which gives
$$
\phi^*(\kappa) = \max\left\{0,\; \frac{1 - M\kappa}{1 + M(1-\kappa)}\right\}, \qquad M = \left[\lambda A_H (1-\kappa)\right]^{-1/(1-\alpha)},
$$ {#eq-phi-kappa}
and reduces to the $\phi^*$ of Proposition 1 at $\kappa = 0$. The pre-switch training fraction is positive if and only if $\kappa^{1-\alpha} < \lambda A_H (1-\kappa)$, which at baseline is $\kappa < 0.571$. This is the answer the extension gives to the concern that $\phi^*$ exists only because compute is immobile: with compute freely redeployed at the switch, the firm still trains before the switch whenever capability built late is worth less than about $57\%$ of capability in place. @tbl-capability reports the solution on a grid of $\kappa$.

| $\kappa$ | $X^*$ | $K^*$ | $X^*/X_E$ | $\phi^*$ | $\underline{\phi}$ | $\tilde{\phi}$ | $V/V_{\text{rec}}$ | Loss, $0.02$ (\%) | Loss, $0.18$ (\%) | Loss, $0.50$ (\%) |

| 0.10 | $4.3 \times 10^{-8}$ | $5.4 \times 10^{-11}$ | $6.2 \times 10^{-6}$ | 0.65 | 0.11 | 0.27 | 0.82 | 29.6 | 2.7 | 28.7 |

: The single firm under pre-positioned capability, at the baseline calibration. $\kappa$ is the effectiveness of capability built after the switch relative to capability in place when it arrives, for an entrant and for the inference capacity an incumbent redeploys to training. $X^*$ and $K^*$ are the pre-switch trigger and capacity of the exact stopping problem with scale chosen whenever the firm invests, and $X_E$ is the trigger of a firm that enters after the switch. $\phi^*$ is @eq-phi-kappa; $\underline{\phi}$ and $\tilde{\phi}$ are the thresholds of Proposition 2 recomputed with the post-switch capability $\phi K + \kappa(1-\phi)K$ (zero when every allocation qualifies). $V/V_{\text{rec}}$ is the firm's value at the demand $X_0 = 0.0046$, half the precommitted-scale trigger of the model of record, divided by the value of the model of record's firm there. The last three columns are the losses of a firm that follows the policy optimal under the belief shown when the true arrival rate is $0.10$, in percent of the informed firm's value at half its own trigger. The first row ("Record") is the model of record with scale chosen at the switch, whose losses are those of @tbl-dilemma. {#tbl-capability tbl-colwidths="[9,13,16,13,5,5,5,8,9,9,9]"}

Four things change relative to the model of record. First, the firm has a finite pre-switch trigger at every $\kappa$ on the grid, where the single firm of the model of record waits for the switch. The level of that trigger is set by $\kappa$ and not by the rest of the calibration: it lies between $10^{-7}$ and $0.15$ of the entrant's trigger, and capacity rises by six orders of magnitude between $\kappa = 0.05$ and $\kappa = 0.30$ (the elasticity of $K^*$ to $\kappa$ is $8.3$ at $\kappa = 0.2$ and $5.5$ at $\kappa = 0.5$). The extension therefore restores pre-switch investment by the single firm without delivering a level for it, and the interval of each parameter on which capacity is interior is the same as under (A2), because the entrant's problem is the post-switch problem. Second, the training fraction falls as late capability becomes a better substitute for capability in place, from $0.68$ at $\kappa = 0.05$ to $0.19$ at $\kappa = 0.5$ and to zero above $0.571$. Third, the faith thresholds fall with it: $\underline{\phi}$ is zero from $\kappa = 0.22$ and $\tilde{\phi}$ is zero at $\kappa = 0.5$, so that at higher $\kappa$ a higher arrival rate lowers the default boundary at every allocation. Fourth, the firm is worth less than the model of record's firm where late capability is worth little ($0.81$ at $\kappa = 0.05$), because the option to enter after the switch is impaired, and more where redeployment is effective ($1.20$ at $\kappa = 1$).

The last three columns give the computed counterpart of the conjecture above for this technology. Both correction channels operate. The pessimistic loss falls from $30\%$ to $4\%$ as $\kappa$ rises to $0.5$, because a firm that trained too little redeploys its inference capacity at the switch; the loss of the far optimist stays at $29\%$ up to $\kappa = 0.3$ and falls to $1.5\%$ at $\kappa = 1$, where pre-switch training is worthless under every belief. For equal errors in $\lambda$ ($0.02$ against $0.18$) the pessimist loses more at every $\kappa$ on the grid, by a factor between $3.0$ and $11$. For equal proportional errors ($0.02$ against $0.50$) the ranking depends on $\kappa$: the two losses are within $4\%$ of each other at $\kappa \leq 0.10$, the optimist loses more at $\kappa$ between $0.2$ and $0.5$ (ratios $0.72$, $0.43$ and $0.22$), and the pessimist loses more at $0.75$ and $1$. So under this technology the asymmetry in levels of $\lambda$ persists and the asymmetry in logs does not, a statement about the grid of @tbl-capability at the baseline calibration and not about the model of record.

**Duopoly Dario's dilemma.** The single-firm exercise (Numerical Finding 1) describes the monopoly case. Here the mismatch is computed inside the entry equilibrium of @sec-duopoly. The benchmark is the equilibrium of Proposition 3(iii) at $\lambda_{\text{true}} = 0.10$, in which one firm leads at $X_L = 0.0034$ with $(K_L, \phi_L) = (0.0042, 0.68)$ and the other follows. One firm holds the belief $\lambda_{\text{invest}}$; its rival holds the truth and knows the mistaken firm's policy. Values are exact under $\lambda_{\text{true}}$ and measured at $X_0 = X_L/2 = 0.0017$, where neither firm is installed; if the switch arrives first, each firm is worth the mutual-waiting value $W$ of the proof of Proposition 3.

*Mistaken leader.* The mistaken firm best-responds, under its belief, to what its rival does. The rival follows, and once it follows it waits for the switch, which is the follower's best response at the true rate in every cell computed. The mistaken leader therefore invests at the demand, capacity and training fraction that maximize its believed value of leading over mutual waiting, the counterpart of @eq-first-investment at its belief, or at once at $X_0$ when that demand lies below $X_0$. For beliefs of $0.075$ and above this is the leader's policy of the equilibrium at that belief (@tbl-duopoly-beliefs), which the computation reproduces to within $0.3\%$ in the trigger; for lower beliefs a rival sharing the belief would enter before the switch, which the informed rival does not do. The informed rival's value of waiting for the mistaken firm's entry exceeds its value of investing first at every demand scanned between $X_0$ and that entry, by the margin in the column "Rival's margin" of @tbl-duopoly-dilemma, so the rival does follow.

*Mistaken follower.* Once the leader has entered, the follower's post-switch policy does not involve $\lambda$, so a mistaken follower that waits for the switch behaves exactly as an informed one and loses nothing. Its belief can matter in two ways. It may enter before the switch, which on this grid it would do only at beliefs at which it does not stay a follower. And before the leader's entry it may take the lead: under its belief it compares leading at the demand it likes best below $X_L$ with waiting for its rival's entry at $X_L$, and it invests first when leading is worth more. Roles then change. The informed firm, which prefers following to leading at these demand levels, follows; the outcome is that of the mistaken leader; and the loss is measured against the benchmark follower's value, which is higher than the benchmark leader's.

Columns two to four give the demand $X$, capacity $K$ and training fraction $\phi$ at which a mistaken firm that leads makes the first investment, starting from $X_0 = X_L/2 = 0.0017$ ($\dagger$: the demand it prefers lies below $X_0$ and it invests at once); the training fraction at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.02$ is the lower bound of the search. "Follower" is the loss of a mistaken firm designated as the follower, in percent of the informed follower's value ($\ddagger$: it takes the lead, at the entry of columns two to four; otherwise it stays the follower). Other parameters: baseline calibration. {#tbl-duopoly-dilemma tbl-colwidths="[8,10,8,6,9,9,10,11,9,10,10]"}

The leader loses on both sides, and more than the single firm of @tbl-dilemma at every belief the two tables share. Allocation is again the largest component. On the pessimistic side the leader's allocation error is larger than the single firm's because a pessimistic leader expects little from a post-switch contest against a follower many times its size: at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.02$ it trains with at most $1\%$ of its capacity and loses $48\%$. On the optimistic side the loss grows faster than for the single firm, $32\%$ at $0.50$ against $13\%$, because the optimistic leader both trains with nearly all of its capacity and installs a capacity that is too large for the early demand at which it enters. The ratios of the pessimistic to the optimistic loss are in @tbl-dilemma-pairs: $27$ in levels, $1.5$ and $5.5$ at factors of five and $1.8$, and $2.3$ in expected time. The informed rival gains when a pessimist leads, by $42\%$ at $0.02$, because a small leader that trains little leaves it most of the post-switch contest, and it loses about $2\%$ when a moderate optimist leads.

The follower's column has a simple structure. For beliefs between $0.075$ and $0.30$ the mistaken follower stays a follower and its loss is exactly zero. For beliefs of $0.069$ and below and of $0.40$ and above it believes that leading at once, or at its own trigger, is worth more than waiting for its rival's entry, and it takes the lead: the believed value of leading exceeds the believed value of waiting by between $2\%$ (at $0.069$) and $124\%$ (at $0.02$). Its loss is then the leader's loss plus what it gives up by not following, between $1.8$ and $3.3$ points. So a mistaken belief can change who invests first, and when it does the case is that of the mistaken leader. Leverage leaves these numbers where they are under fairly priced debt (@tbl-dilemma-tail).

Four limits apply. The mistaken firm's investment region is taken to be the set of demand levels above the demand that maximizes its believed coefficient of leading, as the linear complementarity solve of the proof of Proposition 3 finds for the equilibrium leader; that solve was not repeated at each belief. The rival's preference for following is checked on the demand scan and not between its points. The caveats of Proposition 3(iii) carry over: the benchmark is one asymmetric equilibrium, the symmetric mixed equilibrium is not solved, and the assignment of roles is a selection. And under leverage the policies are the unlevered ones, as in Internet Appendix H.

*Non-equilibrium comparison of the earlier draft.* The earlier draft compared a mistaken firm with a rival that followed its single-firm pure-power policy without best-responding, and measured the loss against symmetric simultaneous entry at that policy, which is not an equilibrium of the entry game. That comparison gives losses of $38\%$ at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.02$ and $17\%$ at $0.20$, against $26\%$ and $6\%$ for the pure-power single firm. It is reported here only so that those numbers can be traced; the corresponding numbers in the equilibrium are the $48\%$ and $2.6\%$ of @tbl-duopoly-dilemma.

**Alternative regime structure.** The binary regime process is a modeling choice, and the concern is that it drives the results. I do not solve the alternative; the discussion below is qualitative. A natural extension replaces the binary process with a three-regime ladder ($L \to M \to H$) in which an intermediate capability level arrives first. The mechanisms of Propositions 1 and 2 would be expected to survive it, because each operates through the composition of $A_{\text{eff}}$: with a second absorbing-direction switch the effective revenue coefficient becomes a longer convex combination of regime-specific continuation values, but it remains increasing in the arrival rates whenever the training fraction is high enough, which is the only property the faith-based survival condition uses; and the training allocation channel behind Dario's dilemma continues to trade L-regime inference revenue against capability-contingent upside. What a third regime would change is quantitative: the value of waiting rises when uncertainty resolves in two steps rather than one, so the trigger $X^*$ and the belief-mismatch losses would both move, and the direction of the net effect on $\phi^*$ is not obvious a priori. The two-regime specification is a modeling choice that captures the feature the paper is about, binary uncertainty over whether AI becomes transformative, rather than a case verified against a richer alternative.

**Endogenizing the arrival rate.** A natural extension would endogenize the arrival rate $\lambda$ as a function of aggregate training compute, so that firms' training investments collectively accelerate the regime switch. I do not solve that extension, and what follows is a conjecture about it rather than a result. Each firm's training would contribute to a common arrival rate, and a decentralized equilibrium would plausibly leave that spillover partly uninternalized, so equilibrium training could fall short of the level a coordinating industry would choose. If so, the two forces run in opposite directions: preemption pushes toward overinvestment in capacity, while the training spillover pushes toward underinvestment in training.

**Testable predictions.** The testable predictions of @sec-discussion could be assessed more fully as the cross-section of publicly traded AI labs expands, though the small sample currently limits formal statistical testing. Default-probability and spread regressions could test prediction 1 using training-share proxies, such as the ratio of pre-training compute to total compute disclosed in some filings; the model predicts no effect of the training share on recovery. Event studies around AI capability and timeline announcements, model releases, benchmark results, and prominent revisions of AGI forecasts, could test the predicted asymmetric response of installed labs' values to timeline news. Cross-sectional regressions could test whether training shares rise with belief proxies while capital expenditure does not move monotonically with them. These exercises require data that are currently scarce but becoming available as AI firms go public and disclosure norms develop.

**Policy implications.** On policy, the faith-based survival mechanism (Proposition 2) sharpens the familiar concern about optimism-supported valuations without endorsing its usual framing. Inside the model nothing is masked: the H-regime option value genuinely raises equity value and genuinely lowers the default boundary, and a firm sustained by that option is correctly valued given its belief. What the mechanism does imply is that solvency depends on a belief parameter, so a downward revision in $\lambda$ would raise the default boundary and cut equity value at once; whether investors' beliefs about AI timelines are themselves accurate is outside the model's scope. On disclosure, a lab's measured training share $\phi^{\mathrm{o}}$ summarizes its intertemporal trade-off between current revenue and future capability, so two labs with identical capital expenditure can carry very different solvency and value composition. Whether requiring standardized disclosure of training allocation would improve any dimension of market efficiency is a question the model cannot address, since it contains no information asymmetry, no belief updating by investors, and no price formation; the claim it supports is narrower, that an investor working inside this model would need $\phi^{\mathrm{o}}$, and not compute spending alone, to locate a lab relative to its default boundary. On competition policy, capacity investment serves two purposes at once, generating revenue and deterring a rival; the model evaluates no intervention and so ranks no policies, and what it supplies is the strategic component of investment that such an evaluation would have to price.

**Financing structures beyond public debt and equity.** The labs whose decisions the model represents finance themselves in varied ways. Some build proprietary infrastructure (e.g., xAI's Colossus supercluster), while others rely on hyperscaler partnerships (e.g., Anthropic--Amazon, OpenAI--Microsoft); in both cases the investment decision resides at the lab level, even when the physical infrastructure is co-owned or leased from a third party. The structural default framework of @leland1994corporate assumes publicly traded equity and continuously tradeable debt, a setting that several frontier AI labs, reportedly financed through SAFE notes, convertible debt, and multi-class equity, do not resemble. The mechanism is best read as a tractable approximation to the broader distress risk these firms face: the default boundary $X_D$ is the demand level at which the firm can no longer sustain operations, whether the binding constraint is a missed coupon, a failed funding round, or a covenant violation. Three qualitative predictions plausibly carry over to other financing structures, though the model solves only one and does not verify the portability: higher training investment lowers the distress threshold through the continuation-value channel, leverage concentrates the tail risk of overinvestment, and the default boundary rises with rival capacity.

**Further limitations of the contest specification.** Beyond the alternative contest functions discussed above, the Tullock contest abstracts from product differentiation, network effects, and switching costs, and it omits the market-growing effect of AI adoption, in which investment expands total addressable demand rather than merely redistributing a given level of industry revenue; this biases the model toward stronger competition effects than a setting in which investment grows total demand.

**Regime reversal.** The regime switch to $H$ is absorbing: once the post-AGI regime arrives, the model does not allow reversal. In practice an "AI winter" scenario is possible; the model abstracts from it.

**International dynamics.** The model treats competition among a fixed set of domestic firms, omitting international dynamics, export controls, and sovereign AI initiatives.

**An empirical companion.** The most natural empirical companion to the model is a formal revealed-beliefs methodology that inverts observed investment decisions to recover implied AI-timeline beliefs; the illustrative inversions in @sec-calibration and @sec-valuation demonstrate the concept but fall short of estimation, which would require additional instruments, proper treatment of the uncertainty in the calibration parameters (particularly $\sigma$ and $\alpha$), and a richer model with dynamic $\phi$ and heterogeneous information.

### F. Single-Firm Illustrations in Regime $H$ {.unnumbered}

Two textbook real-options exhibits illustrate the H-regime sub-problem of @sec-single-firm. Both solve the H-regime problem with revenue $X K^\alpha$, i.e. all installed capacity treated as productive training capacity, which is without loss of generality within the absorbing H-regime, where inference capacity generates no revenue and the standalone optimum is $\phi = 1$; all quantitative results in the paper use the full model with the joint $(K, \phi)$ optimization.

**Option value against the NPV of immediate investment.** @fig-option-value depicts the option value $F_H(X)$ of @eq-option-H alongside the net present value of investing immediately at the scale $K_H^*$ chosen for entry at the trigger (the scale is not re-optimized at each $X$; above $X_H^*$ the re-optimized NPV is larger, as Internet Appendix B records), for the baseline calibration. The option value lies everywhere above the NPV curve, with the gap, the shaded "value of waiting" region, largest at low demand levels. At $X = X_H^*$ the two curves meet tangentially (smooth pasting), and for $X > X_H^*$ the firm invests immediately, so the option value equals the NPV. The figure illustrates the core real-options result: for $X < X_H^*$ the firm strictly prefers to wait, and the value of waiting is the whole of the option value where the NPV is negative (below about $0.36 X_H^*$ at baseline) and still exceeds half the NPV at $X = 0.5 X_H^*$; the option premium factor $\beta_H/(\beta_H - 1) \approx 2.8$ in @eq-trigger-H is its geometric counterpart at the trigger, where the two curves become tangent.

![Option value versus NPV of immediate investment in regime $H$. The solid curve shows the option value $F_H(X)$; the dashed curve shows the NPV of investing immediately at the trigger-optimal scale $K_H^*$, held fixed across $X$. The shaded region is the "value of waiting," the excess of the option value over the NPV. The vertical dotted line marks the optimal trigger $X_H^*$ where smooth pasting holds. Parameters: baseline calibration ($\sigma = 0.25$, $\mu_H = 0.06$, $r = 0.12$, $\alpha = 0.40$, $\gamma = 1.50$).](figures/fig_option_value.pdf){#fig-option-value}

**Comparative statics of the H-regime policy.** @fig-comparative-statics presents comparative statics for the optimal trigger $X_H^*$ and capacity $K_H^*$ with respect to four key parameters. @tbl-elasticities reports elasticities at the baseline for the full model's $X^*$, $K^*$, and $\phi^*$, which are not the H-regime objects plotted here. Panel (a) shows that higher volatility $\sigma$ raises both the trigger and the optimal capacity: as in the full model (Internet Appendix C), uncertainty raises the option value of waiting, so investment occurs at a higher demand level, at which the optimal scale is larger. Panel (b) shows the effect of revenue elasticity $\alpha$: higher $\alpha$ (less diminishing returns) raises the trigger and substantially increases capacity, since the marginal value of additional capacity is higher. Panel (c) shows that greater cost convexity $\gamma$ has a non-monotone effect on both the trigger and the optimal capacity: $K_H^*$ is $0.0107$ at $\gamma = 1.20$, $0.0034$ at $1.35$, $0.0067$ at $1.50$, and $0.035$ at $2.00$, with the trigger tracing a similar U-shape. With the cost scale $c$ held fixed, a higher exponent lowers the marginal cost $c\gamma K^{\gamma-1}$ for capacities below the normalized unit $K = 1$, where the optimum lies, once $\gamma$ is large enough for the exponent effect to dominate the factor $\gamma$. Panel (d) shows that higher operating cost $\delta$ raises both the trigger and the optimal capacity. As Internet Appendix C notes, this panel is a rescaling of the capacity unit rather than an economic sensitivity. What the panel does show is the role of the linear cost floor in creating the interior optimum (@eq-foc-K).

Solid lines (left axis) show the optimal trigger $X_H^*$; dashed lines (right axis) show the optimal capacity $K_H^*$. (a) Volatility $\sigma$; (b) revenue elasticity $\alpha$; (c) investment cost convexity $\gamma$; (d) operating cost rate $\delta$.
