### G. A Normalized Scale-Gap Diagnostic {.unnumbered}

Motivated by @berk1999optimal, this section asks how far a firm's installed base sits from the model's optimal scale, and reports the answer as a unit-free index; @sec-valuation summarizes the result. The scale-gap index $g$ compares two quantities, defined below: the value of the capacity already in place, and the shortfall of that value relative to an optimally sized greenfield project. Expressing the shortfall as a fraction of their sum puts the gap on a $[0, 1]$ scale so that it can be read across calibrations.

The construction is deliberately *not* a growth-option decomposition. It does not measure the present value of future investment opportunities, and the two quantities it compares are benchmarks rather than separable claims on the firm: one is measured gross of sunk investment cost, the other net of it. Their sum is therefore a normalization device rather than a valuation identity, and the resulting fraction is not a share of firm value or of market capitalization. The object of interest is the *shape* of the index in $K/K^*$, which is invariant to the cost normalization $c = 1$ (@sec-calibration); its level at any particular point on the horizontal axis is not.

The two components are the following.

1. **Assets-in-place**: the value of existing installed capacity at current demand, incorporating both L-regime inference revenue and H-regime continuation value through $A_{\text{eff}}$.
$$
V_{\text{AIP}} = A_{\text{eff}}(\phi, K_{\text{installed}}) \cdot X - \frac{\delta K_{\text{installed}}}{r}.
$$

2. **Capacity gap value**: the shortfall of the current installed base relative to the optimally sized project,
$$
V_{\text{gap}} = \max\{\text{NPV}(K^*, \phi^*) - V_{\text{AIP}},\; 0\},
$$
where $\text{NPV}(K^*, \phi^*)$ is the net (of the full investment cost $I(K^*)$) present value of the optimally sized greenfield project. This is a comparative-statics measure of distance to optimal scale, namely how far the firm's gross installed-asset value falls short of the net value of a full-scale deployment. It is not the NPV of incremental expansion from the installed base (which would credit the firm for capacity already sunk), and it is not a forward-looking option value. Because the benchmark nets out the entire investment cost while assets-in-place are gross of sunk costs, the gap reaches zero before $K_{\text{installed}}$ reaches $K^*$.

The value of the possibility of transitioning from $L$ to $H$ does not appear as a third additive term: it is embedded in *both* quantities through the effective revenue coefficient $A_{\text{eff}}(\phi, \cdot)$, which already weights the H-regime continuation value by the arrival rate $\lambda$ and the training allocation $\phi$. The scale-gap index is then
$$
g(K_{\text{installed}}) = \frac{V_{\text{gap}}}{V_{\text{AIP}} + V_{\text{gap}}} \in [0, 1].
$$

@fig-growth-decomposition plots the index using the full model with regime switching: values are computed with the effective revenue coefficient $A_{\text{eff}}$ at the optimal training fraction $\phi^*$, evaluated at demand $1.5 X^*$. Panel (a) stacks assets-in-place (blue, lower band) and the capacity gap (orange, upper band) against installed capacity relative to the optimal level $K^*$. When the firm has little installed capacity ($K/K^* \ll 1$), the gap dominates the stack; as installed capacity rises, assets-in-place increase concavely (diminishing returns) while the gap shrinks. Panel (b) plots $g$, which falls from about 80\% at the left edge of the figure ($K/K^* = 0.01$) to zero at $K/K^* \approx 0.77$; the crossover occurs where the gross value of installed assets overtakes the optimal *net* value, since assets-in-place are measured gross of the sunk investment cost while the benchmark nets it out. At the baseline calibration $g$ equals 50\% at $K/K^* = 0.1$ and 26\% at $K/K^* = 0.3$, so the index runs at roughly 25--50\% over that range; the sweeps in Internet Appendix E report 50--59\% and 25--30\% at those two points when each parameter is moved by $\pm 25\%$ one at a time, and 40--61\% and 16--33\% when all nine are moved jointly, so the band survives both. Because $c = 1$ fixes the cost scale by normalization (@sec-calibration), $K^*$ is not a physical quantity and $K/K^*$ cannot be read off observed compute stocks; I therefore make no claim about which point on the axis describes a given firm, and the content of the figure is entirely the monotone decline and the location of the crossover.

![Normalized scale-gap diagnostic. (a) Stacked plot of assets-in-place (blue, lower band) and the capacity gap (orange, upper band) as a function of installed capacity relative to the optimal level $K^*$; the dotted line marks $K/K^* = 1$. (b) The scale-gap index $g = V_{\text{gap}}/(V_{\text{AIP}} + V_{\text{gap}})$ over the same range, reaching zero at $K/K^* \approx 0.77$. The two components are measured against different benchmarks, one gross of sunk investment cost and one net of it, so their sum is a normalization rather than a valuation identity and $g$ is not a share of firm value. Horizontal-axis levels are not identified, because $c = 1$ fixes the cost scale by normalization. Parameters: full model with regime switching at the optimal training fraction $\phi^*$, demand at $1.5 X^*$, baseline calibration.](figures/fig_growth_decomposition.pdf){#fig-growth-decomposition}

The diagnostic carries no direct asset-pricing implication: the model prices all claims by discounting at a single constant rate $r$ and contains no pricing kernel, so it cannot map a value composition into a beta or an expected return. The related conjecture, that a larger H-regime share of value raises equity betas, is stated in @sec-discussion as a hypothesis to be tested, not as a result derived here.

### H. Credit Spreads and Default Probabilities {.unnumbered}

The formulas, the tables and the figure behind the credit-risk discussion of @sec-valuation are collected here.

**Credit spreads.** For debt with coupon flow $C_D$, the credit spread is:
$$
\text{spread} = \frac{C_D}{D(X)} - r,
$$
where $D(X)$ is the market value of the debt at its issuance demand $X$ (which differs from the default-free value $C_D/r$ because of default risk), $C_D = r_c \ell I(K)$ under par debt and the coupon at which $D(X) = \ell I(K)$ under fairly priced debt, and the reference rate is the model's discount rate $r$ (the WACC), not a risk-free rate.^[The benchmark is the model's discount rate $r$ because all claims are valued by discounting at $r$: a default-free perpetuity with coupon $C_D$ is worth $C_D/r$ and yields exactly $r$, so the spread is zero absent default risk and isolates the default-risk component. The model has a single, risk-adjusted discount rate and therefore cannot separately speak to the term-structure or risk-premium components of observed corporate spreads; the reported spreads are model-implied risk-adjusted objects, the default-risk increment over $r$, and not market credit spreads or yield spreads over Treasuries.] Under fairly priced debt the spread is the coupon rate on the proceeds less $r$. The debt values below are those of the entry game (Internet Appendix B): the boundary is the one of the coupled regime-switching problem, default can occur after the switch at the H-regime boundary, and recovery follows @eq-recovery. Because leverage and the coupon rate are exogenous stress-test parameters (@sec-model), the leverage gradients below describe the model's response to an imposed debt burden at a fixed policy, not an optimally chosen capital structure.

**Default probability.** The probability of default within horizon $T$ is the first-passage probability for GBM hitting the barrier $X_D$:
$$
P(\text{default within } T) = \mathcal{N}(-d_1) + \left(\frac{X_D}{X}\right)^{2\nu/\sigma^2} \mathcal{N}(-d_2),
$$
where $\nu = \mu_s - \sigma^2/2$ with $s$ the regime in which the firm enters, $d_1 = [\ln(X/X_D) + \nu T]/(\sigma\sqrt{T})$, $d_2 = [\ln(X/X_D) - \nu T]/(\sigma\sqrt{T})$, and $\mathcal{N}$ is the standard normal CDF. This is the exact barrier hitting probability for GBM, consistent with the Leland-style first-passage default mechanism in the model. For a firm that enters before the switch the drift is $\mu_L$ and the calculation abstracts from the switch itself, since a switch to $H$ before hitting $X_D$ replaces the boundary by the higher-drift H-regime problem, so the reported figures are upper bounds on the pre-switch default probability; for the follower, which enters after the switch, the drift is $\mu_H$. Since $\mu_s$ is the risk-adjusted (certainty-equivalent) drift, the result is a *model-implied risk-adjusted* first-passage probability, computed under the same convention as the spread calculation. It is not a risk-neutral (pricing-measure) probability, because the model discounts at the WACC rather than at a risk-free rate (see the footnote in @sec-model). The physical-measure probability, using the unadjusted drift, would be lower.

**Credit at the model's own policies.** @tbl-credit-spread and @tbl-credit-pd report the spread and the five-year default probability for debt issued at three entry points, at eight leverage levels and under both debt conventions; @fig-credit-risk plots the same objects on a finer grid. The single firm enters at its precommitted-scale policy of Proposition 1(iii), $(X^*, K^*, \phi^*) = (0.0093, 0.0158, 0.70)$, and is priced as an installed monopolist. The leader enters at the first investment of the unlevered equilibrium, $(X_L, K_L, \phi_L) = (0.0034, 0.0042, 0.68)$, held fixed across leverage while the follower best-responds at each leverage. The follower enters after the switch at its trigger $X_F^*$ against that leader, all capacity in training, with its policy re-optimized at each leverage. Holding the leader's policy fixed isolates the effect of a given debt burden. Under fairly priced debt the re-solved equilibria at $\ell = 0.20$ and $0.40$ change the leader's capacity and trigger by less than $1\%$ and its spread by less than $0.1$ basis points; under par debt the subsidy raises the leader's trigger by $37\%$ at $\ell = 0.40$, and @tbl-duopoly-leverage reports that equilibrium.

Without debt every firm already has a boundary, the shutdown boundary, at which it would stop operating: the single firm enters at $6.46$ times it, the leader at $4.81$ and the follower at $10.3$, and debt carries a spread from the first unit, $22$, $44$ and $4$ basis points in the limit. Leverage raises the boundary through the coupon and widens the spread to $30$, $51$ and $18$ basis points at $\ell = 0.70$ under par debt, and to $43$, $64$ and $25$ under fairly priced debt, whose coupon rate on proceeds is $r$ plus the spread, $12.0\%$ to $12.6\%$ here, about two and a half times the par coupon. The five-year default probability of the leader rises from $0.84\%$ to $1.21\%$ under par debt and to $2.07\%$ under fairly priced debt over the same range. Recovery is between zero and $4.8\%$ of the default-free claim in every cell, so the cap at that claim never binds. The cap at the unlevered asset value binds for the leader at low leverage ($\ell \leq 0.10$ under par debt, $\ell \leq 0.05$ under fairly priced debt), where its boundary is close to its shutdown boundary and the unlevered value there is close to zero; in every other cell the inference business is worth at most $0.94$ of that value. For the single firm it is zero up to $\ell = 0.15$ under par debt, because the coupled boundary lies below the inference business's own shutdown boundary until the coupon raises it; for the leader the boundary is above it from the first unit. The single-boundary closed forms of Proposition 2, evaluated at the same single-firm policy, place the boundary about $3\%$ higher and omit default after the switch; they give spreads of $17$, $20$ and $23$ basis points at $\ell = 0$, $0.40$ and $0.70$ under par debt, below the $22$, $26$ and $30$ of @tbl-credit-spread, and five-year default probabilities of $0.19\%$, $0.30\%$ and $0.42\%$.

Panels (c) and (d) of @fig-credit-risk vary the training fraction at the single firm's and the leader's scale and entry demand, at $\ell = 0.40$, which isolates the allocation's effect on credit at a fixed debt burden; no point other than $\phi^*$ and $\phi_L$ is a policy of the model. Recovery is zero for $\phi \leq 0.6$, where the inference business is worth nothing at the boundary to an owner who may shut it down, rises through both policies, and flattens where the cap at the unlevered asset value binds. The spread falls in $\phi$ over $[0.30, 0.75]$ under both debt conventions, because more training both lowers the probability of default after the switch and raises recovery, and rises again at the highest training fractions, beyond the allocation that minimizes the boundary (the U-shape of Proposition 2).
